origin.namedBy: Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman; first shown by Petrus Plancius
history: Indus is one of the twelve constellations formed from stars charted by the Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman on their voyage to the East Indies in 1595–97. Petrus Plancius first showed it on a celestial globe in 1598, and it first appeared in print in Johann Bayer's *Uranometria* in 1603.

The figure is a man holding a spear in one hand and a bundle of spears in the other, as if hunting. The name is the Latin for an Indian, a word Europeans of the time used loosely for the native peoples they met from the Americas to the East Indies. Nobody recorded exactly whom the navigators had in mind. He may be a man of Madagascar, where the fleet stayed for months and made many of its observations: the early globe and atlas drawings closely resemble an engraving of a Madagascan spearman in the published account of the voyage. He may equally be from the East Indies or southern Africa, or stand for all of these peoples at once.
Later mapmakers changed the pose (Bayer drew him face-on, Bode from behind) but not the idea. No story is attached to the figure.

overview: Indus represents a spear-carrying man, a figure the Dutch navigators drew from the peoples they met on their voyage. It is a long, faint constellation with one 3rd-magnitude star, lying between the bright stars Peacock and Alnair.
howToFind: From Brooklyn only the northern edge of Indus rises. Its brightest star, [[star:α Ind|Alpha Indi]], skims about two degrees above a perfect southern horizon, which in practice means it is not seen. From latitude 30°N and farther south the northern half is usable on September and October evenings; the full length, which stretches far toward the pole, needs the tropics or the Southern Hemisphere.

Find [[star:Peacock|Peacock]], the bright star of Pavo, and [[star:Alnair|Alnair]] in Grus, almost two fists apart. Alpha Indi is one fist due north of Peacock (directly away from the pole), so that Alpha Indi, Peacock and Alnair make a right-angled triangle. [[star:β Ind|Beta Indi]] is half a fist from Peacock on the side toward the pole.
shape: A long, skinny right triangle formed by Alpha, Beta and Delta, a bit more than a fist on its long sides, with fainter stars trailing off toward the pole. Only Alpha survives suburban light; the rest needs a dark sky.

mainStars.note: Magnitude 3.1, an orange giant about 100 light-years away. On old charts it sits by the man's head at the base of his raised spear.
Magnitude 3.7, an orange giant about 600 light-years away, at the right angle of the triangle.

Magnitude 4.7 and unremarkable to look at, but it is one of the Sun's nearest neighbors at just under 12 light-years. It is an orange dwarf, a little smaller and cooler than the Sun, with a pair of brown dwarfs (objects too small to shine as stars) orbiting far out.
Magnitude 4.4, a white star about 98 light-years away that a small telescope shows to be double.

notableObjects.note: A neat double star: a white primary of magnitude 4.5 with a 7th-magnitude companion close beside it.
Worth finding just to look at a star only 11.8 light-years away. It moves across the sky faster than almost any other naked-eye star and will cross into Tucana in a few centuries.

facts: Epsilon Indi is close enough and Sun-like enough that it has long been a favorite target in searches for planets and for signals from other civilizations.
The name has nothing to do with the Indus River; Indus here is simply Latin for an Indian.
